title: Patch a small drywall hole without a patch kit
mechanism_check: Nail holes and dents need filler only; holes up to ~3 inches need a backing; bigger holes need a real patch panel.
Check what's behind the hole before pushing tools in — wiring and plumbing live in walls.
improvised_tools: Spackle, toothpaste (white, in a pinch for nail holes), or baking-soda-thickened white glue.
A putty knife, old credit card, or butter knife as a spreader.
For backing: a paint stir stick or ruler slipped inside and screwed through the drywall.
steps: For nail holes: press filler in with a fingertip, scrape flush with the card, let dry.
For larger holes: slip a stick behind the hole, screw it through the drywall on both sides as backing.
Fill over the backing in thin layers, letting each dry.
Sand lightly and paint; unpainted patches flash through.
stop_conditions: Hole edges crumbling over a wide area: the drywall is water-damaged — find the leak first.
Wiring or pipes visible/touchable behind the hole: stop and map them before cutting anything bigger.

title: Fix a door that drags on the floor
mechanism_check: Dragging comes from: loose hinge screws (door sags), swollen wood (humidity), or settled frame.
Open the door and lift the handle: if the door rises, the hinges are loose — that's the fix.
improvised_tools: Longer screws (3-inch) to bite the framing behind the jamb; wooden golf tees + glue to fill stripped holes.
A screwdriver and a sharp chisel or utility knife for hinge mortise tweaks.
Sandpaper or a hand plane for a swollen bottom edge.
steps: Tighten all hinge screws; replace stripped ones with golf-tee-and-glue + longer screws into the framing.
If the top hinge side still sags, drive one 3-inch screw through the top hinge into the stud.
For swelling: mark the rub spot with chalk, remove the door, and plane/sand the marked area.
Rehang and check the reveal is even around the frame.
stop_conditions: Frame visibly racked or cracked at the corners: the structure moved — shimming hinges won't hold.
Dragging after planing twice: measure — you may be chasing a settling foundation, not a door.

title: Fix a door that won't latch
mechanism_check: Watch the latch meet the strike plate: missing high/low = sag; hitting the plate edge = lateral shift; latch not springing = mechanism.
Chalk the latch bolt and close the door — the chalk mark shows exactly where it lands.
improvised_tools: A metal file or Dremel to enlarge the strike opening in the right direction.
Longer strike-plate screws into the framing; a utility knife to score paint first.
Cardboard shims behind hinges to shift the door laterally.
steps: Chalk the latch, close the door, read where it strikes.
File the strike plate opening toward the mark — small amounts, test often.
If the door sags, fix the hinges (long screws into framing) rather than moving the strike.
Tighten the strike plate with long screws once the latch seats cleanly.
stop_conditions: Latch bolt itself is broken or won't spring: the lockset needs replacing, not the strike.
Door edge split around the latch: the door needs glue/clamp repair first.

title: Silence a squeaky floorboard
mechanism_check: Squeaks are wood moving against a nail or against another board — find the exact board and joist by walking it.
From below (basement/crawlspace) you can see the joist and fix it properly.
improvised_tools: Talcum powder, graphite, or dry soap worked into the seam from above.
Trim-head screws driven through the board into the joist; a stud finder or tapping to locate the joist.
Wood shims + construction adhesive from below to close the gap.
steps: From above: work powder into the squeaking seam and walk it in.
If it persists, locate the joist and drive a trim screw through the board into it at a slight angle.
From below: shim the gap between board and joist with a glue-coated shim.
Snap off or set the shim flush; the squeak is the movement, not the wood.
stop_conditions: Squeak over a wide area with spongy feel: subfloor damage or rot — screws mask a structural problem.
Radiant heat or plumbing under the squeak: verify before driving screws down.

title: Fix a stripped screw hole in wood
mechanism_check: The screw spins because the wood fibers around the threads are torn — the hole needs new fiber, not a bigger screw (usually).
Through-hole vs blind hole changes the fix.
improvised_tools: Wooden toothpicks or golf tees + wood glue (or white glue) as new fiber.
A matchstick bundle for small holes; a dowel for large ones.
Longer or thicker screw as a secondary option once fiber is restored.
steps: Squirt glue into the hole and pack it tight with toothpicks/tees.
Snap them flush, let the glue cure fully (an hour minimum).
Drive the original screw into the restored fiber — it will bite like new.
For heavy loads (hinges), use a glued hardwood dowel instead of toothpicks.
stop_conditions: Particleboard or MDF crumbling around the hole: filler won't hold — use a through-bolt with washers.
Hole in end grain under load: end grain never holds screws well; redesign the joint.

title: Open a window painted shut
mechanism_check: Paint bridges the sash-to-frame joint on the inside and outside; cutting the bridge frees it.
Check for nailed-shut sashes or sash locks engaged before forcing anything.
improvised_tools: A sharp utility knife to score the paint joint inside and out.
A stiff putty knife or painter's 5-in-1 tool as a wedge.
A block of wood + hammer to tap the sash frame (never the glass).
steps: Score the paint line where sash meets frame, inside and outside, top and sides.
Work the putty knife into the joint and lever gently along the length.
Tap the sash rails with the wood block to break the remaining bond.
Once moving, work the sash up and down to clear it, then wax the tracks.
stop_conditions: Glass flexing or cracking sounds: stop — pressure is going through the pane.
Window is a designated egress (bedroom): if it won't free safely, it needs professional freeing — egress is life safety.

title: Fix a wobbly chair or table leg
mechanism_check: Wobble from: loose joinery (leg moves in its socket), uneven leg length, or a racked frame.
Rock it diagonally: the leg that lifts is the short one; legs that shift in sockets are loose joinery.
improvised_tools: Wood glue + clamps (or rope tourniquet as a clamp) for loose joints.
Sandpaper or a hand plane to shorten the long leg; felt pads to shim the short one.
Corner braces or screws for a racked frame.
steps: Identify the cause: loose joint vs uneven legs.
Loose joint: work glue into the joint, clamp tight, wipe squeeze-out, cure overnight.
Uneven legs: set the piece on a flat surface, mark the long leg, shave it down gradually.
Check diagonal rock after each adjustment — sneak up on level.
stop_conditions: Joint wood split or tenon broken: glue alone won't hold — the joint needs pinning or replacement.
Antique or valuable piece: stop and consult a restorer before altering it.

title: Reattach a loose cabinet hinge
mechanism_check: Hinge screws strip out of particleboard/MDF cabinet frames — the substrate is the weak link.
European hinges have adjustment screws: the door may just need adjusting, not remounting.
improvised_tools: Toothpicks + glue in stripped holes; longer screws where the frame allows.
A screwdriver; the hinge's own adjustment screws for alignment.
Epoxy putty as a last-resort anchor in crumbled particleboard.
steps: First try the hinge adjustment screws — most 'loose' doors are misaligned, not detached.
For stripped holes: pack with glued toothpicks, cure, re-drive.
Remount the hinge plate and adjust until the door sits flush and even.
If the particleboard is crumbled, bed the screws in epoxy putty and let it cure before loading.
stop_conditions: Frame material disintegrating over a wide area: the cabinet needs a new mounting block screwed to solid wood.
Hinge cup hole in the door blown out: the door needs a repair plate or replacement.

title: Patch a torn window screen
mechanism_check: Small tears (<3 inches) patch; larger tears or brittle screen need re-screening.
Fiberglass vs aluminum screen: fiberglass patches with adhesive, aluminum needs wire or replacement.
improvised_tools: Clear nail polish or super glue to seal small tears; a patch cut from spare screen + silicone.
A spline roller substitute: a butter knife handle or old credit card edge.
Needle and fishing line to stitch larger fiberglass tears.
steps: Trim frayed edges of the tear.
For small holes: dab clear nail polish over the tear and let it cure.
For larger tears: cut a patch 1 inch bigger all around, glue edges with silicone, press flat.
Stitch + glue for tears under tension near the frame.
stop_conditions: Screen brittle and tearing everywhere you touch it: patching is futile — re-screen the frame.
Frame corners broken: the frame needs re-squaring before any screen work.

title: Remove old caulk without a caulk tool
mechanism_check: Silicone caulk peels; latex/acrylic caulk softens with heat and water; the bond is at the edges.
Old caulk over old caulk never sticks — all of it must come off.
improvised_tools: A sharp utility knife to score both edges of the bead.
A stiff putty knife, painter's 5-in-1, or plastic scraper to lift the bead.
Mineral spirits on a rag for silicone residue; rubbing alcohol for latex residue.
steps: Score along both edges of the old bead with the utility knife.
Get the scraper under one end and pull the bead out in long strips.
Scrub residue with the appropriate solvent on a rag.
Wipe the joint clean and dry before laying the new bead.
stop_conditions: Caulk is actually structural adhesive or the joint is moving: recaulking won't hold — find the movement.
Mold deep in the joint behind the caulk: the substrate needs treating, not just new caulk.

title: Free a stuck wooden drawer
mechanism_check: Drawers stick from: humidity swelling, a loose runner, or contents jammed behind.
Pull gently and feel: even resistance = swelling; one-side catch = runner; sudden stop = jammed contents.
improvised_tools: Candle wax, bar soap, or paraffin rubbed on the runners as dry lubricant.
A spatula or ruler to reach behind and dislodge jammed contents.
Sandpaper for a swollen drawer side (remove the drawer first).
steps: Empty the drawer as much as possible through the opening.
Reach behind with a ruler to push down whatever is jammed.
Work the drawer out with a side-to-side wiggle, never a straight yank.
Once out, wax the runners and sand any shiny rub spots on the drawer sides.
stop_conditions: Runner screws torn out of the cabinet: the runner needs remounting, not wax.
Drawer box joints broken: repair the box before forcing it back in.

title: Hang a heavy picture with no stud finder
mechanism_check: Heavy = needs a stud or a proper hollow-wall anchor; drywall alone holds almost nothing.
Studs sit ~16 inches apart; electrical boxes are nailed to studs — a good reference point.
improvised_tools: Knuckle-tap listening for the solid thunk; a strong magnet to find drywall screws (they're in the studs).
A thin finish nail as a probe — tiny hole, instant answer.
Toggle bolts or snap-toggle anchors for heavy loads on hollow drywall.
steps: Tap along the wall listening for the solid sound; confirm with the magnet finding a screw head.
Probe with the finish nail: solid resistance = stud, hollow = miss.
For studs: drive the hanger screw into the stud. For hollow: use a toggle/snap-toggle rated for the weight.
Hang and check level; heavy pieces get two anchor points.
stop_conditions: Plaster-and-lath walls: magnets and taps lie — probe carefully and use plaster-rated anchors.
Above ~50 lbs on drywall alone: stop and bridge two studs with a cleat.

title: Build a sturdy shelf from scrap lumber
mechanism_check: A shelf fails at the wall connection or by sagging mid-span — brackets carry the load, span sets the sag.
Span rule of thumb: 3/4-inch boards span ~32 inches for books; longer spans need a center bracket.
Find studs for brackets; drywall anchors are for light loads only.
improvised_tools: Scrap 1x or 2x lumber; L-brackets, or wooden cleats screwed to studs.
Screws into studs (preferred) or rated hollow-wall anchors; a level.
steps: Decide the load: books need studs and short spans; decor is forgiving.
Cut the shelf board; sand the edges.
Mount brackets or a rear cleat into studs, checking level.
Set the board, screw it to the brackets, load-test with body weight before trusting it.
stop_conditions: No studs where the shelf must go and heavy load: stop — bridge two studs with a horizontal cleat first.
Board visibly sagging under test load: shorten the span or add a center bracket.

title: Build a pair of sawhorses from 2x4s
mechanism_check: A sawhorse is a beam on four splayed legs; splay gives stability, the top beam carries the load.
Legs splay in both directions (length and width) so it can't tip or rack.
Cross-bracing between legs stops racking under side loads.
improvised_tools: Six 2x4s (or equivalent scrap) per pair; screws or nails.
A saw, a square, and a pencil — layout is the whole job.
steps: Cut the top beam to length (32-48 inches is handy).
Cut four legs per horse with matching angles so they splay both ways.
Attach legs to the beam, then add side stretchers between leg pairs.
Stand it up and check for rock; trim the long leg until it sits flat.
stop_conditions: Horse racking (twisting) under load: stop and add diagonal bracing — unbraced horses collapse sideways.
Using them as scaffolding planks supports: stop — sawhorses are work supports, not scaffolds.
